strengths: Novel orthogonality insight: Empirical observation that SFT and RL parameter updates occupy nearly orthogonal subspaces is well-supported with layer-wise analysis, theoretical justification via concentration of measure, and control experiments validating it's not a high-dimensional artifact
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Consistent improvements across three distinct domains (SQuAD +17.2%, LooGLE +8.0%, ToolBench +10.3%), with strong baselines and ablation studies
Well-motivated problem: Clear demonstration of reasoning-knowledge disconnect with intuitive tool-use example
Practical efficiency: Addresses real challenge of avoiding expensive per-domain RL while outperforming SFT baselines
Extensive reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, prompts, and algorithms across appendices enable reproduction
weaknesses: Overstated domain-agnostic claims: Source and target domains are similar (SQuAD→SQuAD, LooGLE→LooGLE, Movies→other tool categories). No evidence of true cross-domain transfer (e.g., QA skills to tool use). Contradicts central motivation

Limited architectural scope: All experiments use Qwen2.5-7B(Instruct) only. Theoretical claims about orthogonality in high-dimensional spaces need validation across different architectures, model scales, and layer structures

Critical design choices lack justification: (1) Why linear composition θ_final = θ_sft_T + λ·v_skill? No exploration of alternatives. (2) λ fixed at 1.0 despite authors acknowledging suboptimality—no sensitivity analysis. (3) Simple subtraction for skill extraction assumes parameter alignment but doesn't justify why this is optimal

Incomplete theoretical grounding: Figure 2 shows cosine similarity ranging from -0.2 to +0.2, not truly negligible. Appendix C relies on strong assumptions (quasi-isotropic inputs, concentration of measure) that may not hold uniformly. No analysis of theoretical failure cases
Insufficient skill analysis: No interpretation of what v_skill encodes. Which layers matter? How does skill degrade across layers? Layer-specific contributions unexamined

Evaluation metric concerns: Heavy LLM-judge (GPT-4.1) dependency without human evaluation. Synthetic data generation via GPT-4.1 conflates skill transfer contribution with synthetic data quality. Unfair baseline comparisons using extra RL rounds and synthetic data
Missing cross-architecture and cross-task generalization: No experiments validating skills transfer to different model families or different task types (e.g., from QA to tool use)

strengths: Strong empirical results across three diverse tasks (SQuAD +9.9, LooGLE +8.0, ToolBench +10.3%)
Interesting core observation about parameter orthogonality between SFT and RL updates
Well-presented motivation with clear illustrations of the knowledge-reasoning disconnect
Comprehensive experimental documentation and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Includes useful ablations on iterative refinement and transfer strategies
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Orthogonality claim (Figure 2) based on only 5 documents from single dataset (LooGLE); not validated on SQuAD or ToolBench main experiments

Weak theoretical justification: Appendix C derivation is circular (assumes empirical observation to explain it); quasi-isotropic input assumption is hand-wavy; no mechanistic explanation for why orthogonality exists
Linear parameter combination (θ_final = θ_sft_T + λ·v_skill) lacks principled justification; scaling coefficient λ fixed at 1 with zero sensitivity analysis despite paper acknowledging it may vary

Experimental conflation: SQuAD comparison unfairly includes RL on source domain while SEAL doesn't; missing critical ablation comparing against source RL model alone without orthogonality decomposition

Limited true cross-domain transfer evidence: LooGLE uses same dataset for source/target; ToolBench extracts from only one source domain (Movies); claim of domain-agnostic skills unvalidated—no test with different source domains
Limited novelty over prior work: Task vectors (Ilharco et al. 2022) and Zbeeb et al. (2025)'s Reasoning Vectors are nearly identical; core technical contribution is incremental

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: unclear why baseline fails at 0% on some ToolBench categories; no investigation of when/why skill transfer fails; no analysis of what skill vector actually captures beyond vague 'execution logic'
Artificial experimental settings: closed-book QA and tool-use scenarios are somewhat artificial; real systems would use RAG or API documentation
Narrow scope: tested only on Qwen2.5-7B; paper acknowledges architecture generalization as limitation but doesn't test other models; no experiments at different model scales
Heavy reliance on LLM judges: GPT-4.1 as reward function and evaluator; subject to API changes and reproducibility issues over time; no human evaluation
Hyperparameter choices appear ad-hoc: why 2 rounds of iterative refinement? Why these specific document indices? Table 3 mechanism ('content-invariant' learning) vaguely explained

Missing key comparisons: no ablation against frozen RL model with fine-tuned adapter layers; no comparison to simply averaging RL/SFT models; no other parameter arithmetic baselines beyond task vectors

strengths: Novel empirical insight: parameter updates from SFT and RL are nearly orthogonal, well-demonstrated with control experiments and theoretical analysis
Strong and consistent empirical results across three diverse domains (SQuAD +9.9pts, LooGLE +8.0pts, ToolBench +10.3pts average)
Comprehensive experimental scope with rigorous documentation: extensive appendices, detailed hyperparameters, and reproducible procedures enable verification
Thorough ablations validating key design choices: iterative skill refinement (Table 3) and post-hoc composition strategy (Table 4)

Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-3) and well-motivated problem formulation

strengths: Novel insight: empirically demonstrates that SFT and RL parameter updates occupy nearly orthogonal subspaces, providing principled foundation for skill transfer across domains
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse domains (SQuAD, LooGLE, ToolBench) with substantial improvements (SQuAD +9.9pts, LooGLE +8.0pts, ToolBench +10.3pts)
Rigorous ablations including iterative refinement strategy, transfer strategy comparison, and control experiments validating orthogonality claims
Practical efficiency: achieves performance matching 75-step target RL with zero target-domain training time
Strong reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and prompt templates in appendices
Clear motivation with case studies effectively illustrating the knowledge-reasoning disconnect
Theoretical grounding via formal derivation of functional disentanglement from parameter-level orthogonality (Appendix D)
weaknesses: Limited architectural scope: all experiments use only Qwen2.5-7B models; claims about generalization across model families and scales (13B, 70B, different architectures) are unvalidated
Missing empirical comparison with Reasoning Vectors (Zbeeb et al. 2025), the most closely related prior work; only methodological differences are claimed without experimental validation
Critical hyperparameter λ fixed to 1 'for simplicity' despite acknowledged dependence on source-target domain gap; no ablation study on λ sensitivity across domain pairs
Iterative refinement (K×M trade-off) shows high sensitivity (45.3→42.1 accuracy when K increases from 5 to 10); no clear guidance for practitioners on setting these for new domains
Limited analysis of what skill vectors capture: no visualization or interpretation of v_skill; claim of 'content-invariant procedural logic' not directly validated
Theoretical justification incomplete: quasi-isotropic input assumption (Eq. 1) not empirically verified; reliance on unpublished recent work (Zhu et al., Chu et al. 2025)
Evaluation using GPT-4.1 as judge for open-ended QA (LooGLE) and GPT-4o-mini as API simulator may introduce biases; no inter-rater reliability analysis
Cross-domain orthogonality values (10^-3 to 10^-4, Table 11) are near-zero but magnitude interpretation unclear; does this guarantee functional independence?
Limited scope of source domain selection: only single source per benchmark (Movies for ToolBench); no analysis of how orthogonality/transfer varies with source domain choice

strengths: Clear problem motivation: The reasoning-knowledge disconnect is well-articulated with compelling examples demonstrating that SFT memorizes facts without teaching robust execution logic.

Robust orthogonality empirical analysis: Comprehensive validation across tasks, RL algorithms, and reward designs with control experiments (Figure 4) showing orthogonality is not a high-dimensional artifact.
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks (SQuAD +9.9, LooGLE +8.0, ToolBench +10.3 average across 20 categories).
Comprehensive experimental reproducibility: Extensive appendices with detailed hyperparameters, prompts, data generation pipelines, and multi-benchmark evaluation.
Multi-domain evaluation: Testing on short-context QA, long-context QA, and tool-use tasks demonstrates some generalizability.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over Reasoning Vectors (Zbeeb et al., 2025): The distinction amounts to sequential vs. parallel extraction and iterative refinement—methodological choices rather than fundamental insights. The core idea of extracting skill vectors as parameter differences is identical.

Orthogonality is empirical, not theoretical: The paper provides no principled explanation for why ∆W_SFT and ∆W_RL should be orthogonal in general. Appendix D assumes orthogonality rather than deriving it. Results may be specific to the experimental setup (Qwen models, specific domains, particular RL algorithms).

Weak theoretical justification for linear composition: Parameter orthogonality does not automatically justify linear composability in function space. The claim that θ_final = θ_sft_T + λ·v_skill preserves both knowledge and skills lacks formal justification.

Attribution of improvements is unclear: Multiple factors interact (synthetic data quality, iterative refinement, skill injection). Table 1 shows single-round PaST achieves only +11.1 points; the +17.2 gain comes primarily from iterative refinement. Table 6 shows only 1.6-point gap versus target RL, potentially within noise.

Iterative refinement is under-explained and critical to success: This appears essential to performance but is treated as a secondary contribution. K×M trade-off analysis is minimal (Table 4 only on LooGLE). No clear guidance for new domains.

Limited model and domain coverage: Only Qwen 7B evaluated; no testing on GPT, LLaMA, or other architectures. Scalability to 13B/70B models unknown. Single source domain per task; ToolBench uses only Movies.

Static scaling coefficient λ=1: Acknowledged as a limitation but not addressed. No sensitivity analysis or principled method to set λ for new domain pairs. This appears to be a critical hyperparameter.
Insufficient failure analysis: No discussion of when orthogonality assumptions break down or maximum domain distance tolerance. Lack of guidance on applicability boundaries.

Evaluation methodology concerns: SQuAD and LooGLE use GPT-4.1 judge rather than exact match (LLM-dependent); ToolBench uses gpt-4o-mini simulator, not real APIs. No direct comparison with SEAL under identical conditions.

Overclaimed 'domain-agnostic' skill vectors: Vectors are extracted from specific source tasks (Movies, SQuAD passages). Transferability within a domain family ≠ true domain-agnosticism. No evidence for drastically different domains.

Weak statistical rigor: Cosine similarities in Table 10 (~-0.0018) lack confidence intervals or significance tests. Control experiment helps but is not conclusive. High-dimensional near-orthogonality is partially expected.

Unfair baseline comparisons: SEAL and other baseline results taken from prior papers; no identical-setup head-to-head comparison. Different synthetic data strategies and data budgets may confound results.

strengths: Novel empirical observation that SFT and RL parameter updates are nearly orthogonal, enabling modular skill transfer; well-validated across multiple tasks, RL algorithms, and reward designs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct domains (SQuAD, LooGLE, ToolBench) with substantial improvements (9.9, 8.0, 10.3 points) and zero-shot transfer to 20 unseen categories
Exceptional reproducibility with detailed appendices covering hyperparameters, prompt templates, data preprocessing, and evaluation protocols
Clear problem motivation with effective case studies illustrating the functional disconnect between knowledge storage and manipulation
Rigorous ablation studies validating design choices (iterative refinement, transfer strategy, K×M trade-offs) and theoretical grounding in parameter-space analysis
weaknesses: Theoretical gap: Orthogonality is established empirically, but the mechanistic explanation for why this enables cross-domain skill transferability remains underexplored; assumptions in Appendix D (quasi-isotropic activations) are not empirically validated against actual Transformer activations

Severe architectural limitation: All experiments exclusively on Qwen 2.5-7B models; orthogonality may be architecture-specific and generalization to Llama, GPT, and other model families is completely unvalidated

Linear composition oversimplified: Scaling coefficient λ fixed to 1 across all experiments with zero sensitivity analysis; different source-target domain gaps likely require different scaling, but this is unexplored

Confounding experimental design: Both SFT and skill injection phases use synthetic data generation; unclear whether improvements stem from skill vectors or synthetic data quality; no ablation with identical synthetic pipelines across baselines

Weak differentiation from Reasoning Vectors (Zbeeb et al. 2025): Sequential vs. parallel extraction is incremental, and iterative refinement's necessity is shown to help but not proven critical; no direct head-to-head comparison
Statistical rigor: Reported results use single runs or 3-run averages without confidence intervals or significance tests; some margins modest (e.g., 58.7 vs. 58.9 in Table 1)
Limited failure analysis: Inconsistent gains across ToolBench categories suggest failure modes, but when/why skill transfer fails is not systematically analyzed
Non-standard evaluation: SQuAD uses closed-book setting from SEAL; LooGLE judgment via GPT-4.1 introduces unquantified noise; ToolBench uses environment simulator rather than real APIs
